items.title: Concept: attempt first, then compare, then run it
items.body:
The lab's README gives a three-step routine, and it matters more than the answers:

- Read the problem and **write your own attempt before looking at the solution.**
- Compare your attempt with the worked solution. The differences are the lesson.
- Redo hard problems from memory a few days later.

Run the code. The chapter's intro says how: Node or the browser console for most problems, a browser for the few that use `localStorage`, `.mjs` files for the ones that use `import`/`export`, and a network connection for the problems that call a public test API.

Problems build on each other. Later problems reuse names from earlier ones, so paste the earlier solution into the same file before running a later one. For example, the store in the CRUD section grows over several problems.

When a quiz asks "what happens if...", the fastest honest way to learn is to change that one line in your copy and run it.

excerpts.quote: 1. Read the problem. **Write your own attempt before looking at the solution.**

Many problems are cumulative: later ones reuse names defined earlier (e.g. JavaScript 46–47 extend the store from 45; TypeScript 42–50 share the `Project` types from 41). Paste the earlier solution into the same file before running a later one.

readMore.why: The chapter intro listing the browser-only and module-syntax exceptions.

items.title: Why updatePost uses PATCH for a one-field change
items.body:
`updatePost` sends only `{ title: "Edited" }`. The comment in the solution gives the rule: "PATCH = change only these fields; PUT = replace the whole resource". With PATCH the server keeps every field you did not send. With PUT the body *is* the new resource, so a body with only a title could wipe out the post's other fields. Since the goal is a partial update, PATCH is the right verb.

Why the others are wrong:
- The lab's reason is partial versus full replacement, not idempotency.
- PUT can carry a JSON body; the lab notes that "PUT and PATCH follow the exact same shape with a different method".
- Creating is POST in the lab's CRUD mapping ("Create=POST ... Update=PUT/PATCH"); PUT is an update verb.

excerpts.quote: async function updatePost(id, changes) { const res = await fetch(`${BASE}/posts/${id}`, { method: "PATCH", // PATCH = change only these fields; PUT = replace the whole resource headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body: JSON.stringify(changes), });
With GET (29), POST (30), PATCH, and DELETE you now have the full HTTP vocabulary of a CRUD app: Create=POST, Read=GET, Update=PUT/PATCH, Delete=DELETE.
PUT and PATCH follow the exact same shape with a different method.

items.title: Start here: grokjs and the Fable Learning Lab JavaScript chapter
items.body:
grokjs is not an app. It is a large collection of self-study coding lessons in several languages. This pack uses one part of it: the **Fable Learning Lab**, a set of problems with worked solutions. Every quiz here comes from its JavaScript chapter.

Read in this order:

- **README.md** at the repo root, "What This Project Is": a map of all the labs, so you know where the Fable lab sits.
- **Fable Learning Lab/README.md**: the four chapter files, the suggested order, and "How to use it".
- **Fable Learning Lab/01-javascript.md**, top to bottom. Its sections run Fundamentals, Arrays & Objects, Functions in Depth, Async & HTTP, Errors & Robustness, Practical Utilities, then Building a CRUD Data Layer.

Each problem has a **Problem** statement, a **Solution** code block with comments, and a short paragraph after it. The comments inside the code often carry the key idea, so read them, not just the code. Quizzes name the problem they come from by topic (for example the debounce problem or the in-memory store).

excerpts.quote: A self-study problem lab: **200 problems with worked solutions**

Ordered easiest-first. Sections: Fundamentals (1–8), Arrays & Objects (9–18), Functions in Depth (19–24), Async & HTTP (25–32), Errors & Robustness (33–38), Practical Utilities (39–44), Building a CRUD Data Layer (45–50).

readMore.why: The map of every lab in the repo.
The suggested order and how to work each problem.

items.title: Why only "java" is searched after three quick calls
items.body:
`debounce` returns a function that remembers one `timerId` (a closure). Each call does two things: `clearTimeout(timerId)` cancels whatever call was waiting, then `setTimeout(() => fn(...args), delay)` schedules a new one. "j" schedules a search. "ja" cancels it and schedules its own. "java" cancels that and schedules its own. Only the last one is still scheduled, and it runs 300 ms after the last call. The comment: "only this one runs, 300ms after the last keystroke".

Why the others are wrong:
- Timers are not batched; the first two are cancelled.
- Calls are not queued one after another; each one cancels the one before.
- That would be a *throttle* that locks out later calls; this code keeps the last call, not the first.

excerpts.quote: function debounce(fn, delay) { let timerId; return (...args) => { clearTimeout(timerId); // cancel the pending call timerId = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), delay); // schedule a new one }; }
debouncedSearch("j"); debouncedSearch("ja"); debouncedSearch("java"); // only this one runs, 300ms after the last keystroke

items.title: Why the optimistic toggle must copy the task, not flip it
items.body:
`const original = todos` does not copy anything. It is a second name for the same array, holding the same task objects. The solution builds the new list with `todos.map((t) => t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t)`: the changed task is a **new** object, and `todos` and its objects are left untouched. That is why `render(original)` can restore the old state on failure.

If the code instead did `t.done = !t.done` on the existing task, that object is also inside `original`. The "original" would now show the flipped value, and the rollback would show the wrong state. The lab: "Immutability makes the rollback trivial — the old array still exists untouched because we never mutated it."

Why the others are wrong:
- An in-place flip does not call `saveFn` again.
- `render` here just logs the list; it does not compare array references.
- Mutating an array has no effect on a pending promise or its catch.

excerpts.quote: const original = todos; // keep the pre-change list for rollback const optimistic = todos.map((t) => t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t );
} catch (err) { render(original); // save failed -> restore the truth
background, roll back on failure. Immutability makes the rollback trivial — the old array still exists untouched because we never mutated it.

items.title: What fetchWithRetry returns without its final throw
items.body:
Inside the loop, every failure is caught: `catch (err) { lastError = err; ... }`. Nothing is rethrown there. After all attempts, `throw lastError;` is the only line that tells the caller it failed. If you delete it, the function simply reaches its end. An `async` function that ends without `return` resolves with `undefined`. The caller's `.then((todo) => console.log(todo.title))` then runs with `todo` as undefined, and reading `.title` throws a TypeError. That TypeError is what `.catch` logs, not the HTTP error.

Why the others are wrong:
- Nothing rejects, so there is no unhandled rejection; the function resolves.
- The `for` loop stops after `retries` attempts whatever happens.
- The catch inside the loop stores the error; it does not rethrow it.

excerpts.quote: } catch (err) { lastError = err; console.warn(`Attempt ${attempt} failed: ${err.message}`); if (attempt < retries) await wait(500); } } throw lastError; // all attempts exhausted — surface the final error
fetchWithRetry("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1") .then((todo) => console.log(todo.title)) .catch((err) => console.error("Gave up:", err.message));

items.title: What Promise.all does when one request fails
items.body:
`Promise.all` gives you all results or nothing. The solution's comment: "If ANY promise rejects, Promise.all rejects immediately with that error." The `await` throws that error, and the two successful users are not returned. When you want every outcome, use `Promise.allSettled`. It always resolves with one record per promise, either `{ status: 'fulfilled', value }` or `{ status: 'rejected', reason }`. You then filter for the fulfilled ones and keep their values, as `loadTeamSafe` does.

Why the others are wrong:
- Neither function retries anything.
- `Promise.all` rejects at the first failure with that one error, not an array of errors; `allSettled` never throws.
- `Promise.all` does not resolve with a gap; it rejects.

excerpts.quote: // If ANY promise rejects, Promise.all rejects immediately with that error. // When you want every result regardless of failures: async function loadTeamSafe() { const results = await Promise.allSettled([fetchUser(1), fetchUser(-1)]); // [{status:'fulfilled', value:{...}}, {status:'rejected', reason:Error}] const ok = results.filter((r) => r.status === "fulfilled").map((r) => r.value);

items.title: Why createPost needs both JSON.stringify and the header
items.body:
They do two different jobs. `fetch` sends the `body` as it is given, and a plain object is not turned into JSON for you, so `JSON.stringify(...)` makes the string to send. The comment: "body must be a string". The `Content-Type: application/json` header tells the server how to read that string: "tells the server it's JSON". Without it, the server may not parse the body as JSON. The lab lists them among the "Three things beginners forget: the `method`, the `Content-Type` header, and `JSON.stringify` (fetch won't serialize objects for you)."

Why the others are wrong:
- `fetch` does not serialise objects itself.
- `JSON.stringify` does not compress anything; the header describes the format.
- The header does not make `fetch` call `stringify`; you must do it yourself.

excerpts.quote: const res = await fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts", { method: "POST", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, // tells the server it's JSON body: JSON.stringify({ title, body, userId: 1 }), // body must be a string });
Three things beginners forget: the `method`, the `Content-Type` header, and `JSON.stringify` (fetch won't serialize objects for you). PUT and PATCH follow the exact

items.title: Why [10, 1, 5, 25].sort() puts 5 last
items.body:
Without a comparator, `sort` converts the elements to strings and compares them character by character, like words in a dictionary. "1" < "10" < "25" < "5", because "2" comes before "5", and "10" starts with "1". So the result is `[1, 10, 25, 5]`. The comment in the solution says the default sort "compares as STRINGS". For numbers, pass a comparator: `(a, b) => a - b`. Also copy first (`[...nums]`), because `sort` changes the array in place.

Why the others are wrong:
- Array size does not switch the comparison; it is string comparison every time.
- It compares whole strings, not only the first digit.
- Stability is not the issue; the order comes from comparing strings.

excerpts.quote: const nums = [10, 1, 5, 25]; // Default sort compares as STRINGS: "10" < "5". Pass a comparator: const sorted = [...nums].sort((a, b) => a - b); // negative result = a comes first console.log(sorted); // [1, 5, 10, 25]
`sort` mutates in place, so copy first with `[...arr]` (or use `arr.toSorted()` in modern runtimes). Use `localeCompare` for strings and `a - b` for numbers.

items.title: Why removal uses filter instead of splice
items.body:
`splice` changes the array it is called on. `filter` builds and returns a **new** array with the items that pass the test, and leaves the original as it was. React state must be updated with new values, not by changing the old ones, so the lab teaches three shapes: "**add = spread**, **remove = filter**, **update = map + spread**." `todos.filter((t) => t.id !== 2)` is the remove shape.

Why the others are wrong:
- The lab's reason is immutability, not speed.
- `splice` removes by index; you can find the index from an id first, so "cannot remove by id" is not the issue.
- `filter` copies the array, not the objects in it; the remaining todos are the same objects as before.

excerpts.quote: // (b) remove — filter creates a new array without the item const removed = todos.filter((t) => t.id !== 2);
Memorize these three shapes: **add = spread**, **remove = filter**, **update = map + spread**. React state updates use exactly these patterns, so make them automatic now.

items.title: Why let in a for loop gives each callback its own value
items.body:
`let` and `const` are **block-scoped**: each `{ }` block gets its own variable. In a `for` loop with `let`, every pass through the loop gets a fresh binding of the counter. A callback made in pass 2 keeps pass 2's variable, so when it runs later it sees that pass's value. `var` is **function-scoped**: there is only one variable for the whole function, shared by every callback, and by the time they run it holds the final value. The lab: "This is why `let` in a `for` loop gives each iteration its own variable — critical when creating callbacks in loops."

Why the others are wrong:
- `let` does not change when the loop or the callbacks run.
- With `var` the callbacks read the shared final value, not undefined.
- Neither keyword copies values into callbacks. Both are captured as variables; with `let` there is simply a new variable each pass.

excerpts.quote: Each `{ }` block creates a new scope for `let`/`const`. The inner `message` *shadows* the outer one inside the `if` block and disappears when the block ends. This is why `let` in a `for` loop gives each iteration its own variable — critical when creating callbacks in loops. (The old `var` keyword is function-scoped and hoisted; avoid it in new code.)

items.title: Why the arrow callback sees the timer's this
items.body:
In JavaScript, a normal `function` gets its own `this`, decided by *how it is called*. `setTimeout` calls the callback itself, not as `timer.something()`, so inside `function () { ... }` `this` is not the timer object (the lab: `window` in browsers, a Timeout object in Node). `this.seconds` is therefore undefined. An **arrow function** has no `this` of its own; it uses the `this` of the code around it. Inside `start()`, called as `timer.start()`, `this` is the timer, so the arrow reads `this.seconds` correctly. The other fix is `.bind(this)`.

Why the others are wrong:
- The arrow still runs later, when the timer fires, not immediately.
- Arrows are not bound to the object literal; they take `this` from the enclosing function (`start`).
- `setTimeout` passes no object to the callback; the arrow simply uses the outer `this`.

excerpts.quote: // The inner `function () {}` gets its own `this`, set by whoever calls it — here the // timer machinery (`window` in browsers, a Timeout object in Node) — NOT the timer object. // Fix 1 (modern default): arrow functions don't have their own `this`; // they inherit it from the enclosing scope. const timer1 = { seconds: 42, start() { setTimeout(() => console.log(this.seconds), 100); // 42
Rule of thumb: `this` is determined by *how a function is called*, not where it's written — except arrow functions, which capture `this` lexically. Use arrows for callbacks inside

items.title: Concept: from language basics to a small CRUD data layer
items.body:
The JavaScript chapter is ordered easiest-first, and its last section puts the earlier skills together. Knowing the arc helps you see why each early topic is there.

- **Fundamentals** and **Arrays & Objects**: scope, copying and updating arrays and objects, sorting.
- **Functions in Depth**: closures (a function that remembers variables from where it was made), higher-order functions, `this`, debounce.
- **Async & HTTP**: promises, `async`/`await`, `fetch` for each HTTP verb, running requests in parallel, retrying.
- **Errors & Robustness**: custom errors and safe parsing of untrusted text.
- **Building a CRUD Data Layer**: an in-memory task store (create, read, update, delete), then API clients and optimistic updates.

"CRUD" means Create, Read, Update, Delete: the four basic things an app does with data. As you read the CRUD section, look back at which earlier problem each line relies on; the solutions often say so in a comment, such as "private via closure (problem 19)".

excerpts.quote: Ordered easiest-first. Sections: Fundamentals (1–8), Arrays & Objects (9–18), Functions in Depth (19–24), Async & HTTP (25–32), Errors & Robustness (33–38), Practical Utilities (39–44), Building a CRUD Data Layer (45–50).
let tasks = []; // private via closure (problem 19)

items.title: Why getAll returns a copy of the private array
items.body:
`tasks` is private: only the functions inside `createStore` can see it (a closure). The only way to add a task is `add(text)`, which checks the text (`throw new Error("Task text is required")`), trims it, and gives it an id and a date. If `getAll` returned `tasks` itself, the caller would hold the real array and could `push` or `splice` it directly, putting in tasks that never went through `add`'s checks. Returning `[...tasks]` gives a new array, so changing it does not change the store. The comment: "return a copy so callers can't mutate our state".

Why the others are wrong:
- `nextId` is a separate variable; the array does not expose it.
- Returning the real array would give the live array, not a stale one.
- A closure hides the *variable*, but once you hand out the array itself, anyone can change it.

excerpts.quote: let tasks = []; // private via closure (problem 19) let nextId = 1; return { add(text) { if (!text?.trim()) throw new Error("Task text is required");
getAll() { return [...tasks]; // return a copy so callers can't mutate our state },

items.title: What survives a JSON.stringify / JSON.parse round trip
items.body:
JSON can only hold strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays and plain objects. `JSON.stringify` has to turn everything else into one of those, or leave it out:

- A `Date` is turned into its ISO text, such as "2026-...Z". `JSON.parse` gives back that **string**, not a Date.
- A function cannot be written as JSON, so its key is **dropped**.
- A key whose value is `undefined` is also **dropped**.

So the result is `{ date: "2026-...Z" }`, as the solution's comment shows: "Date became a string; functions/undefined were dropped".

Why the others are wrong:
- JSON adds no type tags, so nothing can rebuild the Date or the function.
- `stringify` does not throw on a function; it skips it.
- Functions are not written as source text, and `undefined` keys disappear rather than becoming null.

excerpts.quote: // Bonus: JSON round-trip loses things — know your serialization limits const obj = { date: new Date(), fn: () => 1, missing: undefined }; console.log(JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))); // { date: "2026-...Z" } — Date became a string; functions/undefined were dropped

items.title: Why three awaits in a row take three times as long
items.body:
`await` pauses the function until that one promise settles. Three `await fetchUser(n)` lines in a row mean request 2 does not even start until request 1 has finished, and request 3 waits for request 2. Three requests of about 200 ms each take about 600 ms. With `Promise.all` you start all three first and then wait once for the combined promise, so they overlap and the total is about 200 ms. The solution's comments give exactly these numbers.

Why the others are wrong:
- The event loop does not start a request early; the code calls `fetchUser(2)` only after the first await finishes.
- The two versions take very different time; memory is not the point.
- Sequential awaits are slower, not faster; combining promises costs almost nothing.

excerpts.quote: async function loadTeam() { // Sequential (slow): each await waits ~200ms -> ~600ms total. // Parallel: start all three, await the combined promise -> ~200ms total. const users = await Promise.all([fetchUser(1), fetchUser(2), fetchUser(3)]);
Spotting independent awaits and running them in parallel is one of the easiest real performance wins in a CRUD app (e.g., load the user, their orders, and site settings simultaneously on page load).

items.title: Why the store's remove returns false instead of throwing
items.body:
`remove` counts the tasks, filters out the id, and returns `tasks.length < before`: true if something was deleted, false if not. The comment gives the reasoning: "false = nothing deleted; caller decides if that's an error". Deleting something that is already gone is often fine (for example, a double click on Delete), so the store reports what happened and lets the caller choose. `update` is different: changing a task that does not exist is clearly a mistake, so it throws `NotFoundError`.

Why the others are wrong:
- `remove` never re-inserts anything.
- The comment talks about who decides, not about speed.
- `filter` does not swallow exceptions, and the callback here cannot throw anyway; `remove` returns false by design.

excerpts.quote: remove(id) { const before = tasks.length; tasks = tasks.filter((t) => t.id !== id); return tasks.length < before; // false = nothing deleted; caller decides if that's an error },
update(id, changes) { const exists = tasks.some((t) => t.id === id); if (!exists) throw new NotFoundError("Task", id); // class from problem 34
